transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-08-31 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 47 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Aaron Chen (CTO, Tidepool Labs), Priya Nair (Product), Liam O'Connor (Infra), plus call recording active

Auto-summary (auto): quick syn but may be noisy.

00:00 Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, Jordan from Redwood — thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
00:05 Aaron Chen: Yeah yeah, loud and clear, thanks.
00:08 Jordan Lee: Cool, quick agenda, hi-level we want to run through our quickstart credits, get a sense of your privacy constraints, and then Maya will tee up a short bench and hosting options — hosted, dedicated, private — and what that means for time-to-first-token. Sound good?
00:22 Priya Nair: Yep, good. We're trying to understand how fast we can get a prototype live and then what the path to production looks like, esp for PHI/PII data.
00:30 Maya Patel: Great, I'll jump in on the infra pieces after Jordan does the quickstart flow.

00:45 Jordan Lee: So the most common path we see is self-serve — you sign up, get free credits, call the Redwood API, and you're generating in minutes. We give credits that are usable against hosted inference. If you need a predictable throughput or want isolation we then have Dedicated which is reserved GPU capacity, and Private which is our VPC or on-prem package.
00:58 Liam O'Connor: Quick question — when you say "hosted" what's your data retention and does data hit your control plane? We have compliance needs where some telemetry can't leave the VPC.
01:07 Jordan Lee: Good question. For hosted, request/response metadata is short-lived and we have options to turn off retention; we can provide SOC2 docs and the control plane is multitenant. For restricted workloads we recommend Private (VPC or on-prem) — with VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for keys.
01:22 Aaron Chen: And Dedicated — is that single-tenant hardware or logical isolation? We need predictable latency for certain endpoints.
01:30 Maya Patel: Dedicated is reserved capacity in our infra — it's logically isolated to your account with dedicated GPU pools. You get throughput SLAs and more predictable p99s. If you need network-level isolation we push Private with VPC peering. Dedicated still routes through Redwood's control plane though, unless you opt for the Private package.

01:52 Priya Nair: Our priority is speed to prototype for the product team, but for clinical features we need private. So likely a hybrid, starting hosted for fast iteration then private for PHI. Does that workflow fit your customers?
02:04 Jordan Lee: Absolutely, hybrid is very typical. You can run the early prototype on hosted with our free credits to validate UX, then move the model and traffic to Dedicated or Private once you hit compliance gating. We also provide model pinning and rollouts so you can canary new model versions.

02:20 Liam O'Connor: On the KMS side, do you integrate with AWS KMS and Azure KeyVault? We also have an HSM in our colo.
02:29 Maya Patel: Yes to AWS KMS and Azure KeyVault for Private. For on-prem we support HSM integrations — it's part of the enterprise package. For hosted we manage keys on our side but can provide encryption-at-rest and in-transit certifications.

02:45 Jordan Lee: Let me call out cost/latency levers — batching, prefix/KV caching, and quantization. For many products you can keep latency low and cut unit costs with prefix cache and smaller quantized model variants. But of course there's a quality trade.
02:58 Aaron Chen: Are those controls manual or suggested automatically by Redwood Optimize? We don't have bandwidth to tweak kernels and batch sizes.
03:07 Maya Patel: We have an Optimize toolkit that suggests configs based on your workload distribution — e.g., if you have short prompts we recommend smaller batch sizes and tighter SLOs, if you have high-throughput chat we suggest continuous batching and cached KV. We can run profiling during the pilot and provide recommended configs.

03:28 Speaker 4: (muffled) — sorry, could you repeat the bit about prefix cache?
03:32 Maya Patel: Sure. Prefix/KV cache saves repeated token keys — so repeated system prompts or shared context won't be recomputed. It reduces per-token compute. It's really helpful for agents that reuse a lot of context.

03:50 Aaron Chen: Ok. For the pilot, we're thinking two tracks — 1) core product conversational UX (non-PHI) on hosted for speed and 2) a clinical triage flow (PHI) that will need a private connection. We want to compare latency and cost numbers.
04:05 Jordan Lee: Perfect. For the hosted arm we'll provision credits and the self-serve quickstart link. For the private arm we can either do VPC peering with a short window for benchmarking or spin up a Dedicated pool with network ACLs depending on your timeline.
04:20 Liam O'Connor: How long to set up VPC peering? We can't open inbound to the internet for clinical traffic.
04:27 Maya Patel: VPC peering typically is 1-2 days for simple peering + route tables; if you require private control plane we'll need some architecture sessions — that can be 7-14 days depending on approvals. For a bench run we can also bring a restricted data subset to hosted with DLP and tokenization to measure QoE if you prefer not to do peering first.

04:50 Priya Nair: Timeline — product wants a prototype in 3 weeks to demo to internal stakeholders. Is that realistic?
04:58 Jordan Lee: For a hosted prototype absolutely — most teams can be live within 48–72 hours with self-serve credits. For private rollout that's a longer path as mentioned.
05:08 Aaron Chen: Ok, so the critical gating items: SOC2 evidence, KMS integration options, network setup doc, and cost numbers for Dedicated and Private.
05:16 Jordan Lee: We'll send SOC2 + ISO summary and a short architecture diagram for VPC peering + HSM. I'll also include a pricing snapshot: hosted per-token, Dedicated monthly commit ranges, and an estimated on-prem license.
05:30 Speaker 4: Also curious about function/tool calling and streaming — we have a streaming UX.
05:35 Maya Patel: We support streaming tokens and function-style structured outputs. Streaming is supported in hosted and Dedicated; for Private it's available in the on-prem package too. Performance-wise streaming doesn't add overhead beyond per-token cost.

05:52 Aaron Chen: On the model side, are you bringing curated open models or proprietary Redwood models? We want to know quantization options for smaller models.
06:00 Jordan Lee: We have a model catalog — curated open models and variants with Redwood-verified profiles. We also support quantized variants. For Dedicated and Private you can pin exact model versions. The runtime will pick kernels and quantization settings that match CPU/GPU.
06:15 Aaron Chen: If we run a batch of 1k QPS emulate, will you provide perf numbers?
06:20 Maya Patel: In the benchmark we'll run both p50/p95/p99 and throughput sweeps. For example, with a T4-like pool and a 512 token context we can show p99 under X ms depending on model; we'll deliver a bench report.

06:37 Priya Nair: Ok, let's talk operational handoffs — who will be the Redwood lead for the pilot?
06:42 Jordan Lee: I'll be your AE and will coordinate. Maya will run the bench and be your SE contact. I'll attach their contact emails after the call.

06:50 Jordan Lee: Quick demo of onboarding — sign up, hit the tokens API, we have SDKs, and the Console shows cost per token at a route level, token breakouts so product can see spend.
06:58 Priya Nair: Does Console include tracing for prompt-level outputs? We need to see quality regressions.
07:05 Maya Patel: Yes, Console has per-route dashboards, tracing hooks, and you can tie evals to prompt sets so you get regression alerts. For privacy you can redact or hash PII fields before sending traces.

07:22 Aaron Chen: Any gotchas? We are concerned about warm-up times and cold starts, KV cache hits, and memory for very long contexts.
07:31 Maya Patel: The runtime supports continuous batching and incremental KV caching; for very long contexts we recommend segmenting or using retrieval-augmented flows. Cold starts are minimized with warm pools. For Dedicated we reserve warm capacity, for hosted we have burst policies.

07:50 Liam O'Connor: Pricing — can you give a rough ballpark for Dedicated monthly commit for 4 GPUs vs 16 GPUs?
07:58 Jordan Lee: I'll send concrete numbers but ballpark wise 4-GPU reserved pools start in the low tens of thousands per month and scale; 16 GPUs is a larger commit. Depends on model size and expected throughput. We'll provide a slide with committed capacity pricing and expected cost per 1M tokens under typical configs.

08:15 Priya Nair: About contracts — we have legal that wants a short pilot SOW and an option to convert to Dedicated. Is that supported?
08:22 Jordan Lee: Yes, we commonly do a pilot SOW with conversion terms. I'll loop in our sales ops after the call to draft initial SOW language.

08:35 Aaron Chen: For the pilot data set we'll redact PII, but we might want to test with a synthetic PHI-like dataset to measure latencies. Would Redwood handle that?
08:43 Maya Patel: Yes, we can run bench on synthetic or redacted datasets. If you do VPC peering we can run the bench inside the peered network to emulate production.

09:00 Jordan Lee: Quick recap and actions: we'll provision 20k free credits, send quickstart link, SOC2 + arch diagram, pricing sheet, and schedule an SE bench session for week of Sep 7. Aaron will send a small prompt set and Liam will confirm network constraints.
09:15 Aaron Chen: Sounds good. One more question — do you support SSO/SCIM for large teams?
09:20 Jordan Lee: Yes we support SSO via SAML and SCIM provisioning for user management in Console; we'll include details in the security packet.

09:30 Priya Nair: Great — thanks all. That timeline works for the product team.
09:33 Jordan Lee: Awesome, we'll follow up 1) credits & quickstart, 2) SOC2 + VPC doc, 3) pricing & pilot SOW. Thanks everyone.

09:45 End meeting
